True Statement: The processes which together perform the maintenance job in living organisms are called life processes.

True Statement: Aerobic respiration breaks up the three-carbon pyruvate molecule in the mitochondria to give three molecules of carbon dioxide and water.

False 1: The release of energy in anaerobic respiration is much greater than in aerobic respiration.

False 1: ADP is used to fuel all other activities in the cell and is broken down to give a fixed amount of energy that drives endothermic reactions.

True Statement: The energy released during respiration is used to make an ATP molecule from ADP and inorganic phosphate.
False 1: The energy released during respiration is used to make an ADP molecule from ATP and inorganic phosphate.

True Statement: In aquatic organisms, the rate of breathing is much faster than in terrestrial organisms because the amount of dissolved oxygen is fairly low compared to oxygen in air.
False 1: In aquatic organisms, the rate of breathing is much slower than in terrestrial organisms because the amount of dissolved oxygen is fairly low compared to oxygen in air.

True Statement: Fishes take in water through their mouths and force it past the gills where dissolved oxygen is taken up by blood.
False 1: Fishes take in water through their gills and force it past the mouth where dissolved oxygen is taken up by blood.

True Statement: In human beings, air passing through the nostrils is filtered by fine hairs that line the passage and mucus helps in this process.
False 1: In human beings, air passing through the nostrils is filtered by cilia in the alveoli and mucus helps in this process.

True Statement: Rings of cartilage are present in the throat to ensure that the air passage does not collapse.
False 1: Rings of bone are present in the throat to ensure that the air passage does not collapse.

True Statement: Within the lungs, air passages divide into smaller and smaller tubes which finally terminate in balloon-like structures called alveoli.
False 1: Within the lungs, air passages divide into smaller and smaller tubes which finally terminate in balloon-like structures called bronchioles.

True Statement: When we breathe in, we lift our ribs and flatten our diaphragm, the chest cavity becomes larger, and air is sucked into the lungs.
False 1: When we breathe in, we lower our ribs and dome our diaphragm, the chest cavity becomes larger, and air is sucked into the lungs.

True Statement: During the breathing cycle, the lungs always contain a residual volume of air so that there is sufficient time for oxygen to be absorbed and CO₂ to be released.
False 1: During the breathing cycle, the lungs are completely emptied so that all CO₂ can be released and fresh oxygen taken in.

True Statement: In human beings, the respiratory pigment is haemoglobin, which has a very high affinity for oxygen and is present in red blood corpuscles.
False 1: In human beings, the respiratory pigment is haemoglobin, which has a very low affinity for oxygen and is present in red blood corpuscles.

True Statement: Carbon dioxide is more soluble in water than oxygen and is hence mostly transported in dissolved form in blood.
False 1: Carbon dioxide is less soluble in water than oxygen and is hence mostly transported in dissolved form in blood.

True Statement: Blood consists of a fluid medium called plasma in which the cells are suspended.
False 1: Blood consists of a fluid medium called lymph in which the cells are suspended.

True Statement: Plasma transports food, carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes in dissolved form; oxygen is carried by the red blood corpuscles.
False 1: Plasma transports oxygen; food, carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes are carried by the red blood corpuscles.

True Statement: The heart has different chambers to prevent oxygen-rich blood from mixing with blood containing carbon dioxide.
False 1: The heart has a single chamber which allows oxygen-rich blood to mix with blood containing carbon dioxide.

True Statement: Oxygen-rich blood from the lungs comes to the left atrium, then moves to the left ventricle, and is pumped out to the body.
False 1: Oxygen-rich blood from the lungs comes to the right atrium, then moves to the right ventricle, and is pumped out to the body.

True Statement: De-oxygenated blood from the body comes to the right atrium, is transferred to the right ventricle, which then pumps it to the lungs for oxygenation.
False 1: De-oxygenated blood from the body comes to the left atrium, is transferred to the left ventricle, which then pumps it to the lungs for oxygenation.

True Statement: Ventricles have thicker muscular walls than atria because ventricles have to pump blood into various organs.
False 1: Atria have thicker muscular walls than ventricles because atria have to pump blood into various organs.

True Statement: Valves in the heart ensure that blood does not flow backwards when the atria or ventricles contract.

True Statement: Amphibians and many reptiles have three-chambered hearts and tolerate some mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
False 1: Amphibians and many reptiles have four-chambered hearts and tolerate some mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

True Statement: Fishes have only two chambers in their hearts; blood is pumped to the gills, oxygenated there, and passes directly to the rest of the body.
False 1: Fishes have four chambers in their hearts; blood is pumped to the gills, oxygenated there, and passes directly to the rest of the body.
False 2: Amphibians have only two chambers in their hearts; blood is pumped to the gills, oxygenated there, and passes directly to the rest of the body.

True Statement: Blood goes through the heart twice during each cycle in vertebrates other than fishes; this is known as double circulation.
False 1: Blood goes through the heart once during each cycle in vertebrates other than fishes; this is known as double circulation.
False 2: Blood goes through the heart twice during each cycle in fishes; this is known as double circulation.

True Statement: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and have thick, elastic walls because blood emerges from the heart under high pressure.

True Statement: Veins collect blood from different organs and bring it back to the heart; they have valves to ensure blood flows only in one direction.
False 1: Arteries collect blood from different organs and bring it back to the heart; they have valves to ensure blood flows only in one direction.
False 2: Veins collect blood from different organs and bring it back to the heart; they have thick elastic walls instead of valves.

True Statement: The smallest blood vessels with one-cell thick walls are called capillaries; exchange of materials between blood and cells takes place across this wall.
False 1: The smallest blood vessels with one-cell thick walls are called venules; exchange of materials between blood and cells takes place across this wall.

True Statement: Platelet cells circulate around the body and plug leaks by helping to clot blood at points of injury.
False 1: Red blood corpuscles circulate around the body and plug leaks by helping to clot blood at points of injury.

True Statement: Normal systolic pressure is about 120 mm of Hg and diastolic pressure is 80 mm of Hg.
False 1: Normal systolic pressure is about 80 mm of Hg and diastolic pressure is 120 mm of Hg.

True Statement: Lymph is similar to plasma but colourless and contains less protein; it carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine and drains excess fluid from extracellular spaces back into blood.
False 1: Lymph is similar to plasma but colourless and contains more protein; it carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine and drains excess fluid from extracellular spaces back into blood.

True Statement: In plants, xylem moves water and minerals obtained from the soil, while phloem transports products of photosynthesis from the leaves to other parts.
False 1: In plants, phloem moves water and minerals obtained from the soil, while xylem transports products of photosynthesis from the leaves to other parts.

True Statement: At the roots, cells actively take up ions creating a concentration difference, so water moves from the soil into the root xylem.
False 1: At the roots, cells actively take up ions creating a concentration difference, so water moves from the root xylem into the soil.

True Statement: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of the plant, and helps in absorption and upward movement of water and minerals.
False 1: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of the plant, but it does not contribute to the upward movement of water and minerals.

True Statement: The effect of root pressure in transport of water is more important at night; during the day, transpiration pull becomes the major driving force.
False 1: The effect of root pressure in transport of water is more important during the day; at night, transpiration pull becomes the major driving force.

True Statement: Translocation of food and other substances occurs in the phloem and takes place in the sieve tubes with the help of adjacent companion cells.
False 1: Translocation of food and other substances occurs in the xylem and takes place in the tracheids with the help of adjacent companion cells.

True Statement: Material like sucrose is transferred into phloem tissue using energy from ATP, which increases the osmotic pressure of the tissue causing water to move into it.
False 1: Material like sucrose is transferred into phloem tissue using energy from ATP, which decreases the osmotic pressure of the tissue causing water to move out of it.

True Statement: The excretory system of human beings includes a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra.
False 1: The excretory system of human beings includes a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a ureter.
False 2: The excretory system of human beings includes a single kidney, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra.

True Statement: Each capillary cluster in the kidney is associated with the cup-shaped end of a coiled tube called Bowman's capsule.
False 1: Each capillary cluster in the kidney is associated with the cup-shaped end of a coiled tube called the nephron.

True Statement: Each kidney has large numbers of filtration units called nephrons packed close together.

True Statement: In the initial filtrate, substances like glucose, amino acids, salts and a major amount of water are selectively reabsorbed as urine flows along the tube.
False 1: In the initial filtrate, substances like glucose, amino acids, salts and a major amount of water are all excreted out without reabsorption.
